title: Evaluate the suitability of small stock carcasses and organs for human consumption

lessons.title: Identifying abnormalities in sheep and goat carcasses
lessons.html:
The role of the meat examiner

A meat examiner working under the Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000 and its regulations examines every small stock carcass and its organs and decides, within the limits of their authority, whether they are fit for human consumption. Conditions outside that authority, or cases of doubt, are referred to the responsible meat inspector or veterinarian. The aim is to protect consumers from disease, to stop zoonoses (animal diseases that spread to people), and to support disease surveillance.

Using all the information

  • Ante-mortem findings: animals that were lame, emaciated, feverish, or slaughtered as emergencies need closer post-mortem examination.
  • Systematic post-mortem examination: head, pluck (lungs, heart, liver), viscera, and carcass, using observation, palpation and the prescribed incisions.
  • Carcass condition: setting, colour of fat and muscle, smell, and degree of bleeding.

Common deviations in small stock

FindingTypical location and appearance
Sheep measles (Cysticercus ovis)Small cysts or calcified spots in heart muscle, diaphragm and skeletal muscle
Hydatid cystsFluid-filled cysts in liver and lungs
Liver flukeThickened, calcified bile ducts; flukes in ducts
Thin-necked bladder worm (Cysticercus tenuicollis)Thin-walled cysts on the liver surface and omentum
Lungworm and pneumoniaGrey-red consolidated areas, nodules, adhesions to chest wall (pleurisy)
Caseous lymphadenitisLymph nodes enlarged with green-yellow, layered pus
Abscesses and injection-site lesionsEncapsulated pus in muscle, often neck or hindquarter
JaundiceYellow discolouration of fat, connective tissue and sclera
EmaciationWasted muscle, gelatinous (serous) fat
Bruising and fracturesHaemorrhage in tissue; age of bruise estimated by colour
ContaminationWool, ingesta, faeces, bile

Examiners must distinguish between a localised lesion, confined to one site, and a generalised condition, which affects the whole animal, such as septicaemia, pyaemia with multiple abscesses, generalised jaundice or fever. This distinction drives the judgement.

lessons.title: Formulating and executing the judgement
lessons.html:
Possible judgements

  • Passed as fit for human consumption: no abnormalities, or only trivial ones.
  • Passed after removal of affected parts (partial condemnation): localised lesions such as a bruise, a single abscess, or a fluke-affected liver.
  • Detained: held for further examination, laboratory tests, setting, or referral to the meat inspector or veterinarian.
  • Totally condemned: generalised disease, or conditions that make the whole carcass a risk or repulsive.

Principles behind judgements

  1. Localised versus generalised: a localised lesion with a healthy carcass usually leads to trimming of the affected part; signs of generalisation (several lymph nodes involved, multiple abscesses, fever signs, poor bleeding, oedema) point to total condemnation.
  2. Public health risk: zoonoses and parasites transmissible through meat require stricter action.
  3. Fitness and wholesomeness: carcasses with a strong abnormal smell, severe emaciation or extensive contamination that cannot be removed are unfit even if no disease agent is proven.
  4. Legal standards: the regulations under the Meat Safety Act set out judgements for specific conditions. Apply them as trained, and never go beyond your authority.

Examples

FindingUsual direction of judgement
Single liver with fluke damageCondemn liver; carcass passed if otherwise normal
Hydatid cysts in lungsCondemn affected organ
Cysticercus ovis lesionsJudgement depends on degree of infestation per the regulations; refer if in doubt
Generalised jaundiceDetain or condemn according to the regulations and inspector's decision
Multiple abscesses in carcass and lymph nodesTotal condemnation

Executing the judgement means making sure it is carried out: affected parts trimmed and placed in condemned containers, detained carcasses moved to the detention area and secured, condemned material denatured or secured as required.

lessons.title: Completing the task: marking, records and communication
lessons.html:
Marking

Carcasses passed as fit are marked with the approved inspection mark of the abattoir. Detained carcasses carry a detention tag. Condemned material is identified so it cannot re-enter the food chain. Only authorised persons handle marking equipment, and stamps are kept secure.

Handling condemned material

  • Place in clearly marked, leak-proof condemned containers.
  • Keep condemned material in the lockable condemned room until disposal.
  • Ensure disposal follows the approved method for the abattoir, such as rendering or another approved route.
  • Prevent access by workers, the public and scavengers.

Records

Accurate records are required for legal compliance, owner payment and disease surveillance:

  • Number of animals slaughtered per owner.
  • Conditions found, organs and carcasses condemned, and the reasons.
  • Detained carcasses and their final outcome.
  • Findings that suggest a controlled or notifiable disease under the Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984, reported immediately through the proper channel.

Communication

  • Inform the line supervisor of trimming requirements and recurring dressing faults, such as wool or ingesta contamination.
  • Give feedback to the owner or producer when appropriate: for example, high rates of liver fluke or measles suggest a need for parasite control on the farm.
  • Refer any case outside your competence to the meat inspector or veterinarian.

Hygiene during examination

Sterilise knives and hooks after each carcass and immediately after cutting into a lesion. Wash hands frequently. Protect yourself from zoonoses with intact skin, covered wounds and appropriate PPE.

Key points

  • Use ante-mortem information and a systematic post-mortem routine.
  • Distinguish localised lesions from generalised conditions.
  • Judgements are pass, partial condemnation, detention or total condemnation, according to the regulations.
  • Refer cases beyond your authority to the meat inspector or veterinarian.
  • Secure condemned material and record all findings accurately.

quiz.question: Where are Cysticercus ovis lesions typically found?

options.text: In heart muscle, diaphragm and skeletal muscle

quiz.question: Lymph nodes enlarged with green-yellow layered pus suggest which condition?
A sheep carcass is normal but its liver shows thickened, calcified bile ducts with flukes. What is the usual judgement?

options.text: Condemn the liver and pass the carcass if otherwise normal
Detain the carcass for a week

quiz.question: Which finding points to a generalised condition?

options.text: One small bruise on the leg
A single hydatid cyst in the lung
Multiple abscesses in the carcass and several lymph nodes

quiz.question: What should a meat examiner do with a case outside their authority?

options.text: Refer it to the meat inspector or veterinarian
Ask the line supervisor to decide

quiz.question: Findings that suggest a controlled disease must be reported immediately through the proper channel.
Condemned material may be stored in the general chiller until disposal.
Which are possible judgements for a small stock carcass? (select all that apply)

options.text: Passed as fit for human consumption
Passed after removal of affected parts
Sold to workers at a discount
